paragraphs: A duality gives two mathematical descriptions of the same physical system. Finding one requires more than matching a few outputs: researchers must construct a corresponding Hamiltonian and a mapping between observables in the two descriptions. This paper turns that search into an optimization problem that neural networks can help solve.

The networks parameterize the relevant mappings, while a loss measures differences between correlation functions in the original and proposed dual models. Training therefore seeks descriptions whose correlations agree. This connects a theoretical physics problem to a concrete learning objective, making candidate dual descriptions accessible through numerical optimization.

The framework numerically rediscovers Kramers–Wannier duality for the two-dimensional Ising model, including its known temperature mapping. For an Ising model modified by a plaquette coupling, it finds families of approximate duals. The distinction matters: reproducing a known duality demonstrates the approach on an established case, while the modified model provides approximate correspondences. Discovering new dualities remains a prospective direction.
icml-2025-a-machine-learning-approach-to.tldr: Neural networks turn duality discovery into an optimization problem, recovering a known Ising-model duality and finding approximate duals for a modified model.

paragraphs: Direct alignment algorithms train language models from preferences without a separate reward-modeling stage. Instead, they express reward through the policy being trained. The paper examines a problem in methods such as DPO and SimPO: training can undesirably lower the probabilities of preferred responses, a behavior called likelihood displacement.

AlphaPO introduces an alpha parameter that changes the reward function’s shape beyond the usual logarithmic form. The central idea is that the mathematical relationship between response probability and reward influences how optimization changes the model. Adjusting that relationship gives finer control over likelihood displacement and over-optimization, making reward shape an explicit part of alignment design.

On instruction-tuned Mistral-7B and Llama3-8B, AlphaPO reports roughly 7%–10% relative alignment improvements over SimPO and 15%–50% over DPO. These are relative performance gains for the evaluated models, rather than percentage-point increases. Together with the analysis, the results support systematically changing reward shape as a way to influence training dynamics and improve alignment.
icml-2025-alphapo-reward-shape-matters-f.tldr: AlphaPO adjusts reward-function shape to better control alignment training and improves reported performance over SimPO and DPO.

paragraphs: Language-model alignment can compare groups of helpful and undesirable responses, providing a richer signal than a single preferred–rejected pair. During self-play, however, a model can generate more candidate answers than it is practical to include in training. AMPO addresses the resulting selection problem: which small group should represent that larger pool?

The method combines responses generated by the current policy, a group-based contrastive objective, and active subset selection. It scores responses and represents their meaning with embeddings, then selects candidates covering both reward extremes and distinct semantic clusters. This allows training to include strong and weak answers alongside less explored kinds of responses that might otherwise be overlooked.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees concerning expected reward maximization with its selection method. Experiments report state-of-the-art AlpacaEval results using Llama 8B and Mistral 7B. The contribution is therefore both a training approach and a way to allocate limited preference-training capacity across a large candidate pool, using quality and semantic variety to identify informative examples.
icml-2025-ampo-active-multi-preference-o.tldr: AMPO selects informative, semantically varied response groups from self-play candidates to improve language-model preference optimization.

paragraphs: Gigapixel pathology slides contain enormous numbers of image patches. Full self-attention can model relationships across those patches, but its quadratic computational cost makes it impractical at this scale. Existing shortcuts reduce that cost while sacrificing some of full attention’s modeling capabilities. Querent seeks to retain useful global context through more selective computation.

For each patch, the framework predicts which surrounding regions are likely to matter and computes attention with those potentially important contexts. Efficient summaries of regions and estimates of their importance guide this selection. Because attention is chosen dynamically for each query patch, the approach can focus computation while retaining access to relevant context across the slide.

The authors give a theoretical bound for the approximation to full self-attention. They also evaluate biomarker prediction, gene mutation prediction, cancer subtyping, and survival analysis across more than ten whole-slide datasets, reporting superior performance over state-of-the-art approaches. These findings support query-dependent context selection as a practical way to reduce overhead while preserving detailed relationships between patches.
icml-2025-context-matters-query-aware-dy.tldr: Querent dynamically selects relevant regions for each image patch, approximating full attention efficiently on gigapixel pathology slides.

paragraphs: Selecting valid instrumental variables from observational data is a central difficulty in causal inference. Many existing selection methods concentrate on models with additive linear relationships and constant effects. This paper broadens the setting to additive nonlinear models while retaining the constant-effects structure, allowing the selection problem to cover more complex relationships.

The main theoretical contribution is a testable criterion called the Cross Auxiliary-based independent Test, or CAT, condition. Within the specified model and under the paper’s assumptions, the authors establish that the condition is both necessary and sufficient for identifying valid instrumental-variable sets. That equivalence gives the condition a stronger role than a heuristic indicator, while keeping its validity tied to the stated modeling setting.

The authors turn the condition into a practical selection algorithm and evaluate it on synthetic data and two real-world datasets. They report effectiveness and robustness across those experiments. The work links a characterization of valid instrument sets to a usable procedure, supporting broader causal analysis within additive nonlinear, constant-effects models.
icml-2025-data-driven-selection-of-instr.tldr: A testable condition enables instrumental-variable selection in additive nonlinear, constant-effects models, with necessity and sufficiency established under the paper’s assumptions.

paragraphs: Graph transformers use attention to learn from relationships among graph elements. The paper identifies a spectral limitation: their attention preserves low-frequency feature signals while failing to capture other important signals, including high-frequency ones. Recent approaches partly address this issue, but their filters remain constrained by a predefined graph spectrum or spectral order.

GrokFormer introduces spectral filters whose graph spectrum and order can adapt during learning. It builds these filters through Fourier-series modeling over learnable activation functions. The purpose is to give the model a more expressive way to select and combine graph signals, rather than restricting its filters to a fixed spectral design.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that these filters are more expressive than other spectral methods. Evaluations cover ten real-world node-classification datasets and five graph-classification datasets, with reported improvements over state-of-the-art graph transformers and graph neural networks. The range of domains, scales, and graph properties makes the experiments relevant to whether this added spectral flexibility helps across varied graph-learning settings.
icml-2025-grokformer-graph-fourier-kolmo.tldr: GrokFormer learns adaptive spectral filters to capture graph signals that conventional graph-transformer attention can miss.

paragraphs: Neural image-quality metrics can be manipulated by adversarial attacks. This matters when their scores influence search rankings, benchmark comparisons, or judgments about content quality: an altered score can undermine the reliability of the assessment. The paper studies defenses for these metrics through a broad, systematic benchmarking effort.

The evaluation includes thirty defense strategies spanning purification, training-based approaches, and certified methods. It tests them against fourteen attacks on nine no-reference image-quality metrics. Both adaptive and non-adaptive attack settings are included, allowing defenses to be examined under different relationships between the attack and the protection being evaluated.

The main contribution described is the comparative benchmark itself. Its coverage brings multiple defense families, attack settings, and quality metrics into a shared evaluation effort, providing a basis for assessing protective methods across combinations of conditions. The benchmark also accepts submissions to support further development. The abstract establishes the scope and intended use of this resource without identifying a winning defense or claiming that the evaluated protections eliminate adversarial vulnerability.
icml-2025-guardians-of-image-quality-ben.tldr: This benchmark evaluates thirty defenses against fourteen attacks on nine neural image-quality metrics.

paragraphs: Training can exhaust GPU memory because intermediate activations must be available for later computation. Re-materialization reduces storage by recomputing selected activations when needed, while preserving the exact computation. The challenge is to choose a schedule that saves substantial memory without excessive execution overhead or an impractically expensive scheduling process.

HiRemate handles this planning problem hierarchically. It recursively divides a large computation graph, applies optimized solvers at several levels, and combines their solutions into a global training schedule. This structure allows it to handle substantially larger graphs than earlier integer-linear-programming methods while keeping runtime overhead low.

The framework targets activation re-materialization for single-GPU models and supports networks with thousands of graph nodes. Across the tested networks, the paper reports memory reductions reaching 50%–70% with 10%–15% overhead, while closely approaching optimal solutions and reducing solver time. Integration with PyTorch Autograd requires almost no code changes. Together, these results address both the quality of the memory-saving schedule and the practicality of producing and using it.
icml-2025-hiremate-hierarchical-approach.tldr: HiRemate hierarchically schedules activation recomputation to reduce single-GPU training memory with modest reported execution overhead.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the data a model is expected to handle. Some methods use the geometry of training features to define a suitable distance measure. This paper argues that an uneven distribution of samples can distort that geometry, and that a fixed estimate cannot correct the distortion when new inputs arrive.

The proposed method adjusts the prior covariance matrix using the features of the current input. It reduces covariance along the input-feature direction while restricting the adjustment to the residual space. This restriction is intended to retain essential data characteristics and prevent unintended changes to directions in the principal space.

The method is evaluated with two pretrained models for CIFAR and five for ImageNet-1k, including the self-supervised DINO model. The authors report significant improvements in out-of-distribution detection across the evaluated models. The contribution is an input-responsive correction to the geometry used for detection, showing that information extracted from training data can be refined dynamically when assessing a new sample.
icml-2025-improving-out-of-distribution-.tldr: Dynamic covariance calibration uses each incoming input to refine feature geometry and improve out-of-distribution detection.

paragraphs: Neural networks can approximate functions used to describe physical systems governed by partial differential equations. Scaling this approach to large, high-dimensional problems can demand substantial computation while providing insufficient accuracy. The paper also identifies interpretability as a concern for industrial applications that require precise, understandable models.

INN-TD combines machine-learning methods with ideas from finite elements. Its architecture incorporates interpolation functions with local support, so each such function acts within a limited region. The authors use this structure to obtain sparse learning, linking the network’s representation to the local interpolation approach of finite-element methods.

The paper reports improved accuracy, faster training and solving, and lower memory requirements from this framework. It positions INN-TD for large, high-dimensional parametric PDE problems, including training, solving, and inverse optimization. The approach matters because computational structure and interpretability are built into the representation used to model the physical system. The stated benefits address the combination of scale and precision that motivates the work.
icml-2025-interpolating-neural-network-t.tldr: INN-TD incorporates local finite-element interpolation into a neural framework for more accurate, efficient, and interpretable physical-system modeling.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation can reduce the cost of fine-tuning diffusion models, especially when the pretrained weights are quantized. The paper points out that inexpensive training does not automatically lead to efficient deployment. Existing adaptation recipes need another quantization step after tuning, and that step can noticeably reduce performance at low bit widths.

IntLoRA addresses this mismatch by using integer-valued low-rank adaptation parameters. The original model weights remain quantized during training, helping make fine-tuning feasible on consumer GPUs. At inference, the adaptation weights can be merged directly into the pretrained weights to produce quantized weights for the downstream task, without an additional post-training quantization stage.

This makes the deployment representation part of the tuning design from the outset. It removes the extra conversion step identified as a source of low-bit performance loss. Extensive experiments report significant speedups in both training and inference without losing performance. Those findings support the practical value of coordinating parameter-efficient adaptation with the numerical format the deployed diffusion model will actually use.
icml-2025-intlora-integral-low-rank-adap.tldr: IntLoRA uses integer low-rank updates to fine-tune quantized diffusion models and merge them for inference without post-training quantization.

paragraphs: The paper studies asynchronous time series made up of events at irregular times, with each event described in natural language. This differs from a sequence of measurements taken at evenly spaced intervals. The event descriptions provide semantic information that a language model can use together with the temporal structure of the sequence.

The authors introduce a prompt design tailored to these sequences. Its purpose is to make use of the descriptions’ meaning and the model’s broad world knowledge for reasoning across domains and tasks. The resulting approach covers forecasting, anomaly detection, and data imputation, extending the analysis beyond predicting what happens next.

They also introduce Stochastic Soft Prompting, a prompt-tuning mechanism that reports substantial performance improvements and outperforms fine-tuning approaches including QLoRA. Experiments on real-world datasets report state-of-the-art results across different tasks and datasets. The work combines a representation choice—presenting irregular events through their language descriptions—with a tuning method intended to make that information more useful to the model.
icml-2025-last-stop-for-modeling-asynchr.tldr: A tailored prompt design and Stochastic Soft Prompting help language models analyze irregularly timed, text-described events across several tasks.

paragraphs: Knowledge editing and unlearning aim to change or remove specific information in a language model while preserving its broader abilities. This paper investigates whether identifying the internal mechanisms responsible for a capability can make those changes more precise and robust. It finds substantial differences depending on how the components to modify are located.

The authors distinguish localization based mainly on preserving outputs from localization that identifies higher-level mechanisms with predictable intermediate states. They focus on components associated with a lookup-table mechanism for factual recall. Targeting that mechanism connects the intervention to an internal process involved in retrieving facts, rather than relying primarily on the behavior of final outputs.

Across multiple models and two datasets—sports facts and CounterFact—these targeted interventions produce more robust changes across input and output formats, better resistance to relearning, and fewer unintended effects than baselines. Some localized edits also disrupt latent knowledge more strongly than the compared methods, improving resistance to attacks. These findings support mechanism-aware localization as an important factor in the durability of editing and unlearning.
icml-2025-mechanistic-unlearning-robust-.tldr: Targeting internal factual-recall mechanisms produces more robust knowledge edits and unlearning with fewer reported side effects.

paragraphs: Combining networks can help defend against adversarial inputs, but the usefulness of an ensemble depends partly on how its members differ. This paper asks how to define that diversity and connect it to performance. It first shows that exactly calculating diversity for two networks in this setting is an NP-hard problem.

Under a first-order approximation, the authors decompose adversarial ensemble loss into four components: average individual adversarial loss, gradient diversity, prediction diversity, and cross diversity. They also derive a corresponding decomposition for classification with cross-entropy loss. The analysis shows why gradient diversity alone is insufficient to characterize ensemble diversity within this account: other terms also contribute to the ensemble’s loss.

The theoretical analysis motivates an ensemble method based on orthogonal adversarial predictions, designed to improve gradient diversity and cross diversity together. Experiments validate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution links a more complete, approximation-based description of diversity to a concrete training strategy, while distinguishing that tractable analysis from the hard problem of calculating diversity exactly.
icml-2025-on-the-diversity-of-adversaria.tldr: An approximate loss decomposition shows why adversarial ensembles need more than gradient diversity and motivates a new ensemble method.

paragraphs: Choosing useful training examples becomes harder when data arrives continuously and the complete source cannot be inspected. The paper formalizes this as Incremental Data Selection. A learner must assemble a training dataset of a predefined size while simultaneously learning the task, so selection decisions occur alongside changes in the model.

The authors find that a new example’s effect on the model depends on both its prediction error and its geometric relationship to other data in feature space. PEAKS combines these two signals through prediction error anchored by kernel similarity. Its design makes the relationship between an example’s difficulty and its feature-space position central to deciding whether that example is useful.

Evaluations report that PEAKS consistently outperforms existing selection strategies. On real-world datasets, its performance advantage over random selection also becomes greater as training-data size increases. These findings support using both model error and feature geometry when selecting from a stream, particularly when a fixed dataset budget prevents retaining every arriving example.
icml-2025-peaks-selecting-key-training-e.tldr: PEAKS combines prediction error with feature-space similarity to select useful training examples incrementally from a data stream.

paragraphs: RBench evaluates demanding reasoning across disciplines, languages, and input types. The motivation is that existing benchmarks may not adequately test the nuanced reasoning needed for complex problems, especially when several subject areas or multiple kinds of information are involved. The benchmark targets both language-only and multimodal models.

Its language evaluation contains 1,094 questions spanning 108 subjects, while the multimodal evaluation contains 665 questions across 83 subjects. Questions are available in English and Chinese. Their curation emphasizes calibrated difficulty, balanced subject coverage, and alignment across languages, aiming to create a demanding assessment whose breadth extends beyond a narrow reasoning domain.

The authors evaluate models including o1, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-R1 and report weak performance on complex reasoning, particularly in the multimodal setting. The highest-performing model in that evaluation, OpenAI o1, reaches 53.2% accuracy. This result identifies substantial remaining difficulty on the benchmark even for the strongest evaluated model, supporting RBench’s role as a challenging test of multidisciplinary reasoning.
icml-2025-rbench-graduate-level-multi-di.tldr: RBench tests advanced multidisciplinary reasoning in English and Chinese, revealing substantial challenges especially for multimodal models.

paragraphs: Language models can help identify software bugs without requiring compilation, but auditing an entire repository creates difficulties. Limited context windows restrict how much code they can consider, hallucinations can produce unreliable reports, and extensive analysis consumes time and tokens. RepoAudit organizes this work as an autonomous agent process.

The agent uses memory and explores the repository as needed. Within individual functions, it analyzes data-flow facts along feasible program paths. A separate validator checks those facts and whether the path conditions associated with a suspected bug can be satisfied. These checks aim to reduce false positives by examining the reasoning that supports each potential finding.

On fifteen benchmark projects, RepoAudit finds forty true bugs with 78.43% precision, averaging 0.44 hours and $2.54 per project. It also reports 185 newly discovered bugs in high-profile projects, of which 174 were confirmed or fixed. The results connect repository exploration and validation to practical auditing outcomes, showing both the number of useful findings and the reliability and cost of the reported analysis.
icml-2025-repoaudit-an-autonomous-llm-ag.tldr: RepoAudit combines on-demand code exploration, agent memory, and validation to find repository-level bugs with measured precision and cost.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks use binary spike activations to transmit information efficiently, replacing multiplications with additions. The paper argues that these binary activations can carry too little information, reducing accuracy. Motivated by findings that activation quantization damages accuracy more than weight quantization, it changes where the network uses binary values.

ReverB uses real-valued spike activations with binary weights. According to the paper, this increases activation information capacity while preserving event-driven operation and multiplication-free computation. A trainable factor further allows the binary weights’ amplitudes to adapt during training, increasing the capacity of the network.

At inference, re-parameterization converts the trainable-weight version back into the standard ReverB form to maintain comparable efficiency. Experiments across multiple architectures and both static and dynamic datasets report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is a change in how numerical precision is allocated between activations and weights, together with a way to gain training flexibility without retaining that extra parameterization during inference.
icml-2025-reverb-snn-reversing-bit-of-th.tldr: ReverB improves spiking-network information capacity by pairing real-valued spike activations with binary weights while preserving stated efficiency advantages.

paragraphs: Surface electromyography measures muscle activity for gesture recognition, but real-world noise can make the resulting interactions unreliable. Existing approaches often try to improve resilience through predefined data augmentation. This paper instead learns to enhance short segments of the signal using information already present in its intrinsic patterns.

The proposed Short Term Enhancement Module, or STEM, combines learnable denoising with sliding-window attention. It is designed to integrate into different models and improve noise robustness without manual data augmentation. An efficient attention mechanism using minimal weight-sharing supports the intended inference efficiency, making short-term signal enhancement a reusable component.

The authors insert STEM into a transformer to create STET. Compared with the strongest competing approaches, they report that noise has more than 20% less impact on STET; this describes a reduction in noise impact, not a stated absolute accuracy increase. Results on classification and regression tasks are promising, and experiments show STEM transferring across different gesture-recognition tasks. The findings support learned short-term enhancement as a practical strategy for noisy muscle-signal analysis.
icml-2025-revisiting-noise-resilience-st.tldr: STEM learns short-term enhancement of muscle signals, improving gesture-recognition robustness to noise across models and tasks.

paragraphs: Language models could support social-network interactions, content generation, and communication, but evaluating these abilities through isolated tasks gives only a partial picture. SNS-Bench brings several social-networking tasks into one benchmark so that models can be assessed across a broader collection of relevant text-based activities.

The benchmark covers eight tasks, including classifying notes, judging whether content is relevant to a query, and generating highlighted words in comments. Its 6,658 questions include subjective responses as well as single-choice and multiple-choice formats. This combination broadens the evaluation beyond one answer style and includes both judging existing content and producing task-specific text.

The authors evaluate more than twenty-five language models and observe performance differences across model sizes, with results following a scaling-law pattern. The reported finding connects model scale with performance within this benchmark. SNS-Bench’s main value is the shared assessment structure: several social-networking abilities can be examined together, providing evidence for further development of language-model techniques for these services.
icml-2025-sns-bench-defining-building-an.tldr: SNS-Bench evaluates language models on eight social-networking tasks using 6,658 questions and varied answer formats.

paragraphs: In collaborative software development, an agent’s understanding can fall behind changes to the shared codebase. Acting on that outdated understanding can cause failures and integration problems. SyncMind defines this out-of-sync challenge, focusing on whether language-model agents can recover when their view of the environment no longer matches its current state.

The accompanying SyncBench contains 24,332 scenarios derived from twenty-one popular GitHub repositories, with executable tests for verification. This provides a concrete setting for measuring recovery. The evaluation also examines willingness to collaborate and how agents respond to resource considerations, extending the assessment beyond whether a code change eventually succeeds.

Reported performance varies substantially, from at most 3.33% for Llama-3.1 agents to at least 28.18% for Claude-3.5-Sonnet. Collaboration willingness stays at or below 4.86%, although collaboration is positively correlated with recovery success when it occurs. Small performance differences under resource-aware recovery conditions also suggest limited resource awareness and adaptability. These findings identify coordination and adjustment to changing conditions as significant weaknesses in the evaluated agents.
icml-2025-syncmind-measuring-agent-out-o.tldr: SyncMind and SyncBench measure how coding agents recover from outdated codebase knowledge, revealing weak collaboration and resource adaptability.

paragraphs: Temporal knowledge-graph completion requires representing how facts depend on time. This paper separates two perspectives: diachronic information describes how facts vary across time, while synchronic information describes how relations influence one another within a particular temporal context. The authors argue that treating time as supplementary misses these distinct features.

TeDS represents both perspectives using quaternions. For synchronic modeling, it reorganizes time and relation quaternions into two combined representations and uses the Hamilton operator to model their interaction. For diachronic modeling, it maps time points to angles, applies trigonometric functions to form timestamp representations, and uses the Hamilton operator to rotate relations.

These operations integrate temporal information directly into the relation representations while preserving the distinction between change across time and interactions within a time context. Across six benchmarks, TeDS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models in the reported experiments. The results support using complementary temporal representations when completing knowledge graphs, with the model architecture explicitly designed around both kinds of temporal structure.
icml-2025-teds-joint-learning-of-diachro.tldr: TeDS uses quaternion representations to jointly model changes across time and interactions within temporal contexts for knowledge-graph completion.

paragraphs: A constrained contextual-bandit learner observes context, chooses actions, and tries to accumulate reward while respecting constraints. This paper introduces Optimistic³, which applies optimistic design to three linked parts of that process: learning parameters, making the primary decision, and adapting the dual variables associated with constraint violations.

Within an efficient primal-dual architecture, the framework achieves regret and constraint-violation bounds that grow as the square root of the number of rounds, up to logarithmic factors. Without Slater’s condition, this improves on prior bounds growing with the three-quarter power. When that condition holds, it also removes a previous inverse dependence on the condition’s parameter, delta.

The delta improvement matters because the parameter can become arbitrarily small for difficult constraints, making the earlier bound much larger. The authors also extend the framework to classical multi-armed bandits with stochastic and adversarial constraints. That extension recovers established best-of-both-worlds guarantees with substantially less computational overhead, combining improved contextual-bandit bounds with a more efficient route to existing guarantees in another setting.
icml-2025-triple-optimistic-learning-for.tldr: Optimistic³ coordinates optimism across learning, decisions, and constraint adaptation to improve constrained-bandit guarantees and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Keypoint-guided image generation gives users control over object poses, but existing methods struggle beyond humans and with overlapping people and animals. The paper attributes these difficulties to both the conditioning methods and the available training data. It addresses the two issues together through a new model and dataset.

UniMC is a diffusion-transformer framework that packages instance-level and keypoint-level conditions into compact tokens. These include class labels, bounding boxes, and keypoint coordinates. Explicitly representing such attributes helps distinguish separate objects and their classes, addressing ambiguity in methods that rely on skeleton images as the conditioning input.

The accompanying HAIG-2.9M dataset contains 786,000 images and 2.9 million human and animal instances, with keypoints, bounding boxes, and detailed captions. Manual inspection supports annotation accuracy. Experiments demonstrate the dataset’s quality and UniMC’s effectiveness, particularly under heavy occlusion and in scenes containing multiple classes. The work connects clearer control representations with annotated data suited to learning those controls across humans and animals.
icml-2025-unimc-taming-diffusion-transfo.tldr: UniMC combines explicit object and keypoint tokens with a large annotated dataset to improve controlled generation of humans and animals.

paragraphs: Rectified flow matching generates samples by moving them from a source distribution toward a target distribution along a learned velocity field. At inference, this movement is computed by integrating an ordinary differential equation. Training constructs target directions by linearly interpolating between randomly paired source and target samples.

Different training pairs can imply different directions at the same location. The paper identifies this as ambiguity, or multiple modes, in the target velocity field. Standard mean-squared-error training averages those directions into one prediction, so the learned field does not preserve the multiple alternatives present in the training targets.

Variational Rectified Flow Matching instead learns and samples from multiple possible flow directions. Its central contribution is therefore a change in how directional ambiguity is represented. Experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet produce results the authors describe as compelling. These evaluations support investigating multimodal velocity modeling across several data settings, while the stated findings do not specify a universal improvement over classic rectified flow matching.
icml-2025-variational-rectified-flow-mat.tldr: Variational Rectified Flow Matching learns multiple possible flow directions instead of averaging ambiguous training directions into a single velocity.
